animated_text_intro: Text that comes in one letter or one word at a time. Screen readers get the whole line.
animated_text_preset_a_heading: For a page title, inside a `Heading` so the page still has a heading there.
animated_text_preset_a_long_sentence: A sentence long enough to wrap. It breaks across lines where plain text would while the words come in.
animated_text_preset_a_sentence: For a sentence that comes in a word at a time.
animated_text_preset_after_a_wait: For text that should come in after something else on the page.
animated_text_preset_basic: For a short line like a greeting. The letters come in one after another.
animation_intro: Fades, slides, zooms or blurs its child in, and out again when `in` turns off. The motion is CSS, and it adds no element of its own.
animation_preset_a_card: A card that slides up from below as it comes in.
animation_preset_after_a_wait: For something that should come in a moment later.
animation_preset_basic: A small badge that fades in.
animation_preset_one_after_another: For a few things that come in one by one.
badge_intro: A small label for a status, a count or a tag. `variant` is the look and `level` is the meaning, the same as on [Button]({{docs}}components/action/button). Text that doesn't fit on one line ends with an ellipsis.
badge_preset_a_date: For a date next to a post or a change.
badge_preset_basic: For a short status next to something, like marking an item as new.
badge_preset_count: For a number, like unread messages.
badge_preset_tags: For tags people can click, like filters.
badge_preset_with_a_label: For a name and a value together, like a version number. The colon after the name is added for you.
badge_preset_with_an_icon: An icon before the text, sized to it.
breadcrumb_intro: Where a page sits, on one line. When the line runs out of room, the crumbs fold into a menu one at a time from the start, and a crumb with no link of its own is left out of the menu. The page's own name truncates only once every crumb has folded.
breadcrumb_preset_basic: Every crumb fits, so all of them show. A crumb with no page of its own, like Knives, shows as plain text.
breadcrumb_preset_narrow: In a narrow box, the first crumbs fold into a menu one at a time until the trail fits. A crumb with no link is left out of the menu.
breadcrumb_preset_with_siblings: A crumb can list every page at its level, itself included. They show in the folded menu, so a reader can go across without going up first.
bubble_intro: One message in a conversation. `BubbleGroup` lists several messages in the order they were sent.
bubble_preset_a_conversation: Two people talking. The reply sits on the other side, so you can tell who said what.
bubble_preset_a_reply_to_pick: For a message that does something when clicked, like a suggested reply.
bubble_preset_one_after_another: Several messages from the same person, grouped together.
bubble_preset_with_reactions: For showing how people reacted to a message.
button_intro: Use a button when clicking it does something, like sending a form or opening a dialog. If it takes the user to another page, use a [HyperLink]({{docs}}components/action/hyper-link) instead.
button_preset_basic: The everyday button. Its label says what happens when you click it.
button_preset_busy: While an action runs. `aria-disabled` keeps the button in the tab order and announced, where `disabled` would take it out.
button_preset_copies_a_value: For text the user will paste somewhere else, like an install command. After a click it says Copied for a moment.
button_preset_copies_icon_only: Without `showLabel`, only the icon shows, and screen readers still hear its name.
button_preset_icon_after: For a button that moves the user on, like Next.
button_preset_icon_before: An icon in front of the label makes the action easier to spot.
button_preset_icon_only: For an action everyone knows by its icon, like closing a panel. Give it an `aria-label` so screen readers can say what it does.
button_preset_icons_both_sides: For a button that does two things, like Save and continue.
button_preset_opens_a_menu: Keeps less common actions out of the way. Clicking it opens a menu, and the down arrow shows that it will.
button_preset_with_a_count: For a button with a number on it, like unread messages.
calendar_intro: A month grid for picking a day or a range. [DatePicker]({{docs}}components/input/date-picker) is the same calendar behind a button.
calendar_preset_already_picked: For a calendar that opens on dates chosen before, like an existing booking.
calendar_preset_basic: For picking one date, like a delivery day.
calendar_preset_range: For picking a start and an end date, like a trip. The first click picks the start and the second the end.
calendar_preset_weekdays: For dates that can't fall on a weekend, like a meeting.
card_intro: A surface for one thing, like a summary, a form or a setting. It has no element of its own, so `is` says which one it is: an `article`, a `section` or a list's `li`. Header, content and footer are all optional.
card_preset_action: For a card with a menu or quick action next to its title.
card_preset_basic: The usual card, with a title and description on top and a button at the bottom.
card_preset_dense_header: For a card that's only a title.
card_preset_footer: For a question with buttons to answer it, like confirming a delete.
card_preset_header_only: For a short summary with nothing under it.
checkbox_intro: A native checkbox for turning one option on or off, or picking several from a list. `CheckboxGroup` holds which boxes of a group are checked, and with `selectAll` a box above them checks or clears them all.
checkbox_preset_a_group: Several options under one question, where people can tick more than one.
checkbox_preset_basic: The usual checkbox with its label beside it. Clicking the label ticks the box too.
checkbox_preset_in_a_form: For a box a form needs ticked, like accepting terms. It has no label prop, since its text is its name, so it goes in a `FormItem` with its message.
checkbox_preset_no_visible_label: For a box whose meaning is clear from what's around it, like a row in a table. `aria-label` gives it a name for screen readers.
checkbox_preset_select_all: For a list where people often want everything. The box on top ticks or clears the rest, and looks partly ticked when only some are.
checkbox_preset_with_an_error: For a box that has to be ticked, like accepting terms. The box and the message turn red.
combobox_intro: A text field with suggestions under it. It opens as the field is focused or typed in and closes on Escape or when focus leaves. Pass `open` to decide yourself when it shows. In a form, the field takes its `label` like any other, and picking a suggestion should set the field's value.
combobox_preset_above: For a field near the bottom of the screen. The list opens above it, and starts open here so you can see it.
combobox_preset_basic: A city search. The list narrows as you type, and picking a city puts it in the field.
combobox_preset_form: A city field in a form. Picking a city sets the field's value, and Save shows an error if what's typed isn't on the list.
components_home_get_started:
## Get started

The design system is a Module Federation remote called `design`. Import `design/core` once, before anything else, then import components from `design/components` and routing from `design/router`.
components_home_intro: The components, styles and icons Ki.CL is built from. Each page shows one component live: pick a preset, toggle its props, and copy the code for what you see.
components_home_part_3: Props like `variant`, `size` and `level` set how a component looks. [Layout]({{docs}}components/layout/layout) props set how things are arranged, and `kicl-*` utility classes cover the rest. A view only writes its own CSS when none of those can do the job.
date_picker_intro: A button that opens a calendar and shows the date picked: one day, or a range. `label` puts its name above it and `description` a hint below.
date_picker_preset_a_range: For a first and last day, like the dates of a trip.
date_picker_preset_basic: For a single date, like a start date. The button shows a prompt until a day is picked.
date_picker_preset_in_a_form: For a date in a form. Saving without one shows the error under it.
date_picker_preset_own_format: For a date shown your own way, like with the month written out.
date_picker_preset_own_placeholder: Shows your own prompt on the button before a date is picked.
date_picker_preset_starts_on_a_date: For editing a date that was saved before.
date_picker_preset_with_a_label: For a date with its name above it and a hint below. A click on the name opens the calendar.
date_picker_preset_with_an_error: For a date that has to be picked and wasn't. The button's border, the name and the message turn red.
details_intro: Shows a summary and hides the rest until the user opens it. It's a native `<details>`, so it opens and closes without script, and it's always open when printed.
details_preset_basic: A question with its answer hidden underneath, like one entry in an FAQ. Click the question to show the answer.
details_preset_gap: For an answer with several paragraphs.
details_preset_group: For an FAQ where only one answer is open at a time.
details_preset_own_marker: For a summary with its own look, like a badge.
diagram_intro: Draws boxes, stores, queues and arrows from an object listing each box, where it sits and the arrows between them, in the site's colors and type so it follows the theme.
diagram_preset_active: Highlights in green the part that's working right now, for a diagram that follows something as it runs.
diagram_preset_basic: A few boxes joined by arrows, like a request going from the browser to the database. You place each box yourself.
diagram_preset_edges: Arrows can be dashed, coloured, labelled or point both ways.
diagram_preset_failed: Outlines the part that broke in red.
diagram_preset_groups: Draws a labelled frame around boxes that belong together, like the servers in one region.
diagram_preset_legend: Explains what the colours and line styles mean, with a caption underneath.
diagram_preset_shapes: Besides the plain box there's a cylinder for a store and a queue for jobs.
diagram_preset_table: For a database table. Each line in the box is one of the table’s columns, with its type and an optional key or note.
dialog_intro: Opens over the page and keeps focus until it's closed. Use it when the user has to answer something before going on. It's a native `<dialog>` opened as a modal.
dialog_preset_basic: A title, some text and a close button. Escape or a click outside closes it too.
dialog_preset_close_icon: Swaps the X on the close button for another icon.
dialog_preset_footer: For a question the user has to answer, like confirming a delete.
dialog_preset_full_screen: For a task that needs the whole window. It fills the screen, and the close button stays in its corner.
dialog_preset_keyboard_only: There’s no close button and a click outside does nothing, so Escape or the button in the footer closes it.
dialog_preset_long_content: For more than fits on the screen. It scrolls, and the close button stays in view as the heading scrolls away.
dialog_preset_no_title: For a dialog that only shows something, like a picture. Without a header, name it with `aria-label`.
dialog_preset_not_closable: For a message the user has to acknowledge. Neither Escape nor a click outside closes it, only the button in the footer.
form_intro: A native `form` wired to [react-hook-form](https://react-hook-form.com). Each field's label, description and error point at its control, so a screen reader reads them together.
form_preset_basic: A short sign-up form. Both fields are required, so pressing Create account with one empty shows an error under it.
form_preset_built_by_hand: The same field written out from its parts, for a control without a `label` prop or a layout of your own.
form_preset_contact: Checks each field as soon as you leave it.
form_preset_profile: For editing a saved profile, where no field is required.
frame_intro: Frames a section that fills the window. It's inset by a gap on every side, with rounded corners, and its top follows the site header as it shows and hides. On load it eases from the window's full height into the frame, after `delay` milliseconds, and keeps its width throughout.
frame_preset_basic: A frame needs the whole window, so it opens in a full-screen dialog, and eases in each time it opens.
heading_intro: A title, from `h1` to `h6`. `is` sets its place in the outline and `lookLike` its size, so the two can differ.
heading_preset_basic: The page's main title, an `h1` that looks like one.
heading_preset_small_section_title: For a section title that should look smaller than its level.
heading_preset_two_headings: A section title with a smaller one under it, an `h2` then an `h3`.
home_motivation_accessibility_is_part_of:
## Accessibility is part of the system

Accessibility isn't a layer added after the components are finished.

The system should start with native semantics, preserve keyboard behavior, expose meaningful names and states, and support predictable focus and interaction.

But native HTML is a starting point, not a guarantee. Content, visual contrast, responsive layouts, dynamic updates and custom interactions still need to be designed and tested.

Accessibility should be considered throughout research, design, implementation and testing. Automated checks are useful, but they cannot determine whether every interaction makes sense to a person using assistive technology.

[Accessibility first]({{docs}}patterns/inclusion/accessibility-first) goes through what to check at each step, from research to code.
home_motivation_configuration_you_can_un:
### Configuration you can understand

The system should be approachable to anyone who knows HTML and CSS, even if they haven't memorized a framework-specific API.

The relationship between markup, styles, props and rendered output should be easy to follow.

Avoid unnecessary build-time magic and hidden behavior. Overrides should work with the normal CSS cascade, and component APIs should expose meaningful choices rather than recreate the entire browser through props.
home_motivation_css_that_reads_as_css:
### CSS that reads as CSS

Use the language directly.

Design tokens, custom properties, logical properties, container queries, cascade layers and nesting should make the system easier to understand and maintain.

A small, deliberate set of utilities is useful when it improves composition. A large vocabulary of opaque class names isn't a substitute for understanding stylesheets.

You should be able to inspect a component's CSS and understand why it looks and behaves the way it does.
home_motivation_over_engineering:
### Over-engineering

A button becomes a React component wrapping a headless primitive wrapping a context provider, with props that reimplement what HTML already provides.

Sometimes semantics are lost along the way. A link becomes a clickable `div`. A dialog requires manually rebuilding behavior the browser already provides. Focus handling, validation and interaction states become responsibilities of the component library rather than capabilities we can rely on from the platform.

Not every abstraction is bad, and complex interactions sometimes need custom behavior. The problem is abstraction without enough benefit to justify its cost.

JavaScript ends up doing work the platform already does.
home_motivation_platform_first:
### Platform-first

HTML and CSS are the primitives. Components compose native elements; they don't replace them without a reason.

If the browser already provides the behavior we need, start there: focus, form validation, dialogs, popovers, scrolling and other built-in capabilities.

JavaScript is the exception that has to justify itself, not the default starting point.
home_motivation_predictable:
### Predictable

Components should behave the way their underlying platform primitives and documented APIs lead you to expect.

Keyboard interaction, focus, validation and browser behavior should not come as surprises.

Consistency matters, but consistency alone isn't enough: a consistently broken component is still broken. When a component behaves unexpectedly, treat that as a problem to investigate and fix, not a quirk users must learn.
home_motivation_see_the_implementation:
## See the implementation

The workshop is part of the design system, not a separate gallery. Every example renders the real component.

On a component page, pick a preset and change its props. The example updates, and under it you can read the code that produces it and the HTML it renders. Because the examples are live, you can also use them with a keyboard or a screen reader. The token pages list the CSS variables and utility classes the components are styled with.

The goal is to make the relationship between the API, HTML, CSS and behavior visible.
home_motivation_semantic_by_default:
### Semantic by default

The right element for the job.

Links are links. Buttons are buttons. Forms use form controls. Structure and behavior should be expressed through HTML rather than reconstructed through generic elements and event handlers.

Accessibility starts with correct semantics and native behavior, then carries through content, visual design and interaction. ARIA supplements native semantics when necessary; it isn't a substitute for choosing the right element.
home_motivation_the_principle:
## The principle

The browser already provides a remarkably capable platform.

A design system should help us use it well: establish consistent decisions, make common patterns easier to reuse and keep the implementation understandable.

It should reduce complexity rather than move it somewhere harder to see.

Native elements first. CSS that reads as CSS. JavaScript only where the browser can't do the job.

That's the system I'm building.
home_motivation_the_underlying_problem:
### The underlying problem

Both frustrations come from the same place: too much distance between the developer and the platform.

You configure the abstraction instead of understanding the underlying behavior. When something goes wrong, you debug layers of indirection rather than HTML or CSS.

The abstraction becomes another system to learn, maintain and work around.

I wanted a system where the abstractions earn their place.
home_motivation_the_wrong_relationship_w:
### The wrong relationship with CSS

One approach gives you no useful shared conventions. Every style is bespoke, spacing values are reinvented, and nothing composes consistently.

The other pushes so much styling into utility classes that CSS itself becomes difficult to see. You have to memorize a vocabulary of class names to understand what a component looks like, and the markup stops communicating the structure and intent of the page.

Both approaches can work. Neither is the balance I want.

I want shared conventions without losing the ability to read the stylesheet, understand the cascade and reason about the browser's behavior.
home_motivation_why_i_built_it:
## Why I built it

Design systems come with different trade-offs, regardless of the tools used. But two problems keep coming up.
hyper_link_intro: A link to another page, another site or a spot on the same page. If clicking it does something instead of going somewhere, use a [Button]({{docs}}components/action/button).
hyper_link_preset_an_email_address: A `mailto:` link opens the mail app, in the same tab.
hyper_link_preset_another_site: A link to another site opens in a new tab, and screen readers are told that it does.
hyper_link_preset_basic: The plain link you'd put inside a sentence.
hyper_link_preset_home: For the link back to the home page: `HomeLink`, a house with the look of a button, its name read by screen readers or shown beside it.
hyper_link_preset_icon_after: Puts an icon after the text, like the arrow on a Next link.
hyper_link_preset_icon_before: Puts an icon in front of the text, like the logo of the site it goes to.
hyper_link_preset_icons_both_sides: The logo says where the link goes and the arrow says it opens another site.
hyper_link_preset_looks_like_a_button: For a link that should stand out, like a call to action. It looks like a button but stays a link.
hyper_link_preset_the_current_page: A link to the page you're on is marked as the current page: its underline is heavier, and it can't be clicked.
image_intro: An image with a spinner while it loads and a placeholder if it fails. It fills whatever box it's given.
image_preset_basic: For a wide picture like a page banner. Nothing sets the box's height, so it keeps the picture's own shape.
image_preset_fails_to_load: What shows when the file is missing. A warning icon takes the picture's place, and screen readers still get the `alt` text.
image_preset_own_placeholder: Swaps the warning icon for one of your own.
input_group_intro: A field with icons, text or buttons inside its border. With a button it's a `fieldset`, the default, since a label can't hold a button; with only icons or text it's a `label` (`is='label'`). For one field with an icon, a prefix or a unit, `Input`'s `before` and `after` build this for you.
input_group_preset_a_label: Only an icon and text around the field, so the group is a label, and a click anywhere in it focuses the field.
input_group_preset_a_primary_button: For the one action the field is for, like sending a message.
input_group_preset_a_textarea: For a longer message, growing with what's typed while the button stays beside it.
input_group_preset_basic: An icon, the field and a button that acts on it. A button can't sit in a label, so the group is a fieldset, and disabling it disables both.
input_intro: A single-line text field. `label` puts its name above it and `description` a hint below. `before` and `after` put an icon or a short text, like a prefix or a unit, inside its border. A field with a button is an `InputGroup`. The email, password, search and copy inputs are ready-made versions of both.
input_preset_a_file: For picking a file. The browser draws its own button inside the field.
input_preset_basic: What the user sees before typing. The placeholder hints at what to enter.
input_preset_copy: For a link or token the user needs to copy. The field can't be edited, and the button copies the whole value even when it's cut short.
input_preset_email: For an email address. Phones show the email keyboard and the browser can fill in a saved address.
input_preset_filled: For a field that opens with a saved value, like editing a profile.
input_preset_in_a_form: For a field in a form, with its rule on the `FormField` . Saving it empty shows the error under it.
input_preset_password: For a password. The eye button shows what was typed and hides it again.
input_preset_search: For searching. A button to clear the field shows up once there's text in it.
input_preset_with_a_button: For a field with one action, like sending a message.
input_preset_with_a_label: For a field with its name above it and a hint below. A click on the name focuses the field.
input_preset_with_a_prefix: For the part of a value the user doesn't need to type, like the https:// of an address.
input_preset_with_a_suffix: Shows the unit next to a number, so the user knows what they're entering.
input_preset_with_an_error: For a field that failed a check. Its name, border and message turn red, and a screen reader reads the message with the field.
input_preset_with_an_icon: An icon at the start shows what the field is for at a glance.
layout_intro: Puts its child on a grid and sets the direction, gap, alignment and tracks. It only adds classes to the child; there's no wrapper element.
layout_preset_basic: Puts things one under another, like the fields of a form.
layout_preset_columns: Lays things out on 12 columns. On phones every item is full width.
layout_preset_fill: For cards of equal width: four a row here, one a row on phones.
layout_preset_frames: Gives each item its own width. Here the button is as wide as its label and the search field takes the rest.
layout_preset_row: Puts things side by side, like the buttons at the bottom of a dialog.
layout_preset_wrap: For tags and other things of different widths. They sit in a line and move to the next line when they run out of room.
list_intro: A `ul` or `ol` laid out as a grid, with `ListItem` for each row. Both take [Layout]({{docs}}components/layout/layout) props, so the list sets its direction and gaps and each row lays out its own content.
list_preset_a_grid: For cards in as many columns as fit.
list_preset_a_row: For a few short items in a line, like the tools a project uses.
list_preset_a_row_that_wraps: For a long run of short items, like these component names. They move to the next line when the row runs out of room.
list_preset_alignment: Cards of different heights side by side. Each stretches to the tallest until `alignItems` lines them up at the start, centre or end instead.
list_preset_rows_with_columns: For a checklist with an icon on each line.
list_preset_steps: For steps that have to happen in order, numbered 1, 2, 3.
markdown_intro: Renders Markdown with the design system's own components. One line renders inline, so put it inside the `Text`, `Heading` or `ListItem` that holds it. A whole document renders as headings, paragraphs and lists.
markdown_preset_a_code_block: Three backticks on their own lines make a block of code.
markdown_preset_a_document: More than one paragraph renders as blocks: `#` for a heading, `-` or `1.` for a list, `>` for a quote and `---` for a rule. A heading's level is its number of `#`, so pick the one that fits the page.
markdown_preset_a_link: Turns `[text](url)` into a link. A link to another site opens in a new tab.
markdown_preset_an_image: For a picture, with its description in the square brackets.
markdown_preset_basic: Makes text bold with `**` on each side, or italic with `*`.
markdown_preset_code: For commands and names inside a sentence. Wrap them in backticks and they show as code.
markdown_preset_code_with_a_look: Colours code by what it means, like the state of a job. Put confirm, error, info, warning or secondary in braces straight after it, as in `{'`DONE`{confirm}'}`.
markdown_preset_strikethrough: Crosses out text that's no longer true, like an old date. Wrap it in `~~`.
markdown_preset_warnings: Flags something deprecated or removed. `{'{warning}'}` and `{'{error}'}` after the code show it in those colours.
menu_intro: A group of commands in a native `menu` element, in a row by default.
menu_preset_a_toolbar: Icon buttons packed close together, like the formatting bar of a text editor.
menu_preset_basic: The actions for one thing, like the buttons under a photo. Each button keeps its own look, like the red Delete.
menu_preset_save_or_cancel: The buttons at the bottom of a form.
menu_preset_stacked: Puts the actions one under another, like the list in a dropdown.
navigation_intro: A list of links to other pages in a `nav` element. The items slide in one after another when it appears, in browsers that support `sibling-index()`.
navigation_preset_as_buttons: Links that look like buttons, for a few that should stand out.
navigation_preset_basic: A list of pages one under another, like a sidebar.
navigation_preset_in_a_row: Puts the links side by side, like the links in a site header.
navigation_preset_steps: For links that go in order, like the steps of a guide.
navigation_preset_the_current_page: The link to the page you're on is marked as the current page.
page_indicator_intro: A column of dots at the edge of the window, one for each full-screen section of the page. Each dot links to its section and shows the section's name when hovered or focused. The current dot grows as its section scrolls by. It's fixed to the window, so there's no preview here.
pattern_accessibility_first_build:
## Build

Then check the result the way people will use it.

- Test with the keyboard alone. Everything should be reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus ring.
- Test with a screen reader: VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, NVDA on Windows, TalkBack on Android.
- Zoom to 200% and check that nothing is cut off or overlapping.
- Run an automated check too, but don't stop there. It can't tell whether a name makes sense or an order is logical.
pattern_accessibility_first_content:
## Content

The words on a page, and the order they come in, decide whether people can follow it.

Give every page a title, and every dialog too. Someone who can't see a transition relies on the title to know where they've landed. A `Dialog` takes its name from its `header`.

Use headings to give the page a structure. Screen reader users move between headings to skim, so pick each heading's level for its place in the outline, and use `lookLike` if it should look bigger or smaller.

Write plainly: short sentences, everyday words, and acronyms spelled out the first time.

Keep the reading order the same as the visual order. If a total updates when an option changes, put the total after the options, where focus will reach it next.

Give everything that isn't text a text alternative. An image needs `alt` text, and a button with only an icon needs an `aria-label`.
pattern_accessibility_first_interaction_:
## Interaction and motion

Not everyone uses a mouse, has a steady hand or reads at the same pace.

Make controls at least 24px, and bigger where you can, especially on touch screens. A button, or a link styled as one, is easier to hit than a short text link.

Avoid time limits. Where one can't be avoided, let people extend it.

Anything that moves on its own for more than five seconds needs a way to pause or stop it. Motion should also stop when someone turns on reduced motion in their system settings. [Reduced motion]({{docs}}tokens/accessibility/reduced-motion) lists what the components already do.
pattern_accessibility_first_intro:
Accessibility determines who can use your product, how independently they can use it, and how much effort it takes.

A button that only works with a mouse excludes someone navigating by keyboard. An unlabeled control leaves a screen reader user guessing. An error communicated only through color can leave someone unaware that anything went wrong.

These aren't unusual edge cases. They're ordinary interface decisions that work for some people and create barriers for others.

Accessibility is about removing those barriers. It's about letting people understand information, navigate an interface and complete tasks without unnecessary obstacles.

It's also an engineering concern. When accessibility is considered from the start, it shapes research, content, design, component APIs and testing. When it's postponed until after launch, the same problems can be spread across components, pages and user journeys, making them harder and more expensive to fix.

The goal isn't to add accessibility to a finished product. It's to build a product that works for more people from the beginning.

pattern_accessibility_first_research:
## Research

Accessibility starts with who you learn from.

Include disabled people in research from the start. Ask the questions you'd ask anyone, then add a few about how they get around: which assistive technology they use, what slows them down, and what workarounds they rely on.

Recruiting can take longer, so plan for it.
pattern_accessibility_first_start_with_t:
## Start with the system

The best place to start is often the browser itself.

Native HTML elements already provide much of the behavior accessible interfaces need: keyboard interaction, focus handling, accessible names, states and form validation.

Using those elements consistently also makes behavior more predictable across the product.

When a requirement isn't met by your existing components, look for a native element before building a custom one. A `<dialog>`, `<details>`, `<input type="date">` or native form validation may already solve much of the problem.

Native elements aren't automatically accessible in every context, but they're a stronger starting point than rebuilding browser behavior without a good reason.

From there, accessibility becomes part of every step of development.
pattern_accessibility_first_visual_desig:
## Visual design

Visual design decides whether people can read the page at their own size and in their own conditions.

Body text is 16px and secondary text 14px, and the smallest size is 12px. [Contrast and size]({{docs}}tokens/accessibility/contrast) has the details.

Size things with rem and the column scale rather than fixed pixel widths. Then the page reflows to a 320px-wide window without scrolling sideways, and text can be zoomed to 200% without anything being cut off.

Don't rely on color alone. An error needs words as well as red, and `FormMessage` and `Status` both say what went wrong.

Small text needs a contrast of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text 3:1. The edges of controls and focus rings need 3:1 as well.

Dark mode helps people with light sensitivity and anyone reading at night. You get it by using the color roles instead of fixed colors.
pattern_feedback_and_status_announce_wit:
## Announce without moving focus

Text that appears on its own has to be announced, or a screen reader user may never know. Put it in a live region that's on the page before the message arrives: `role='status'` waits for a pause, and `role='alert'` speaks straight away. Keep `alert` for errors, since it interrupts whatever is being read.
pattern_feedback_and_status_intro: Feedback tells people what the system is doing: that it's working, that something finished, or that something went wrong and how to fix it.
pattern_feedback_and_status_match_the_ur:
## Match the urgency

Make the feedback as prominent as the moment needs. A saved setting needs a quiet line of text next to it. A failed payment needs an error the person can't miss. Something that can't be undone needs a dialog that asks first. If everything interrupts, people learn to dismiss it without reading.
pattern_feedback_and_status_more_than_on:
## More than one channel

Never let color carry the message alone. Pair it with words, and an icon where it helps, so it still works for someone who can't tell red from green, has the screen dimmed, or is listening with a screen reader. `Status` gives each level an icon and text as well as a color.
pattern_feedback_and_status_preset_savin: Turn the switch on and off. While it saves, the line beside it says so; when it's done, it says that too. The line is a `role="status"` region, so a screen reader hears each change without moving.
pattern_feedback_and_status_preset_sendi: Press Send. The first try fails on purpose: the button shows it's working, then an error `Status` says what happened and offers a way out. Try again succeeds.

pattern_feedback_and_status_show_progres:
## Show progress where it started

Put a loading state on the control that started the action, and change its label to say what's happening. A spinner in a corner of the page is easy to miss, and a screen reader won't announce it unless it's in a live region.
pattern_input_and_forms_ask_for_less:
## Ask for less

- Leave out anything you don't need. Each extra field is more work, and some people stop before the end.
- Use the right input type, so phones show the right keyboard and browsers can fill it in: `EmailInput`, `PasswordInput`, `type='tel'`, `inputMode='numeric'`.
- Set `autoComplete`, so returning people don't type their address again.
- Offer a choice instead of typing when the answers are known.
- Split a long form into steps, and let people save and come back.
pattern_input_and_forms_errors:
## Errors

- Check a field when the person leaves it, not on every keystroke.
- Put the error under the field, in words that say how to fix it. `FormMessage` does this and links it to the field.
- Keep the submit button enabled. Pressing it shows what's missing; a disabled button just leaves people guessing why.
pattern_input_and_forms_group_what_belon:
## Group what belongs together

Wrap related radios and checkboxes in a `fieldset` with a `legend`. `RadioGroup` and `CheckboxGroup` do this, so a screen reader announces the question when someone moves into the group.
pattern_input_and_forms_intro:
Forms are where people get things done, so every extra field or unclear label makes the job harder.

Build forms with the `Form` component. It renders a real `form`, so pressing Enter submits it. It turns off the browser's own validation pop-ups, which look different in every browser and vanish after a few seconds, and `FormMessage` shows each error under its field instead.
pattern_input_and_forms_label_every_fiel:
## Label every field

Every field gets a visible `label`, not just a placeholder. A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types, is usually too faint to pass contrast, and isn't a reliable name for assistive technology. Put hints in `FormDescription`, which the field points to with `aria-describedby`.
pattern_input_and_forms_preset_choices_a: Change the delivery or the extras and watch the total. Each group is a `fieldset` with a `legend`, and the total comes after the choices, where focus reaches it next.
pattern_input_and_forms_preset_sign_up: Press Create account with the fields empty, then fill them in. Each error sits under its field and says how to fix it, and the button never turns off.

pattern_modality_intro:
Some tasks are short enough to do without leaving the page: confirming a delete, picking filters, reading a short note. A layer shows that task over the page, or opens it in place, and puts the person back where they were when it's done.

Only some layers are modal. A modal layer pauses the page behind it until it closes. The others leave the page usable.
pattern_modality_preset_a_short_note: The info button opens a `Popover` beside the price. It doesn't block the page: click anywhere else or press Escape to close it.
pattern_modality_preset_confirm_a_delete: Delete a draft. A `Dialog` asks first, takes focus, and gives it back when it closes. After deleting, Undo puts it back.
pattern_modality_preset_filters: Open Filters and turn some on. The button at the foot of the `Sheet` says how many results you'll get, and the list behind changes only when you press it. Closing the sheet another way drops the changes.
pattern_modality_preset_in_place: Not every detail needs a layer. Each `Details` opens in the page, and the page doesn't move away.
pattern_modality_references:
## References

- [MDN, dialog](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog)
- [MDN, Popover API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API)
- [W3C WAI, Dialog (Modal) pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/)
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Modal and nonmodal dialogs](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/modal-nonmodal-dialog/)
pattern_modality_what_the_platform_does:
## What the platform does

`Dialog`, `Sheet` and `Popover` are built on the browser's own `dialog` element and `popover` attribute, so the browser does most of the work. A modal `dialog` gives you, without any script:

- Focus moves into the dialog when it opens, and back to the button that opened it when it closes.
- Escape closes it.
- The rest of the page can't be reached with Tab while it's open.
- It sits in the top layer, above everything, without a `z-index`.

A popover sits in the top layer too, and closes on Escape or a click outside. A sheet that isn't modal is a manual popover, which the browser doesn't close on Escape, so the component handles Escape itself. `Details` isn't a layer: it opens in the page.
pattern_modality_when_to_use_one_part:
## When to use one

Use a layer for a task with a clear start and end that doesn't need the page behind it: confirming a delete, editing a few settings, picking filters. If the person is moving on and won't come back, take them to a new page instead. If they need to look at the page while they work, don't cover it.
pattern_modality_which_layer:
## Which layer

- **`Dialog`** for a decision that has to be made now. It's modal: the rest of the page can't be used until it closes.
- **`Sheet`** for a longer task, like filters or a form, sliding in from an edge. By default the page stays usable beside it. With `modal`, or at tablet width and below, it's modal too.
- **`Popover`** for a short note or a few options next to what opened it. It isn't modal, and clicking outside closes it.
- **`Details`** when the content can just open in the page. It doesn't need a layer at all.

Give every layer a title, so someone who can't see it appear knows what it's about.
pattern_screen_readers_announce_what_cha:
## Announce what changes

Content that appears without the person moving to it, like a saved message or an error, has to be announced. A live region does that: `role='status'` is read when the reader pauses, `role='alert'` straight away. `Status` uses `status` for information and warnings, and `alert` for errors.
pattern_screen_readers_group_and_hide:
## Group and hide

- **Keep what belongs together in one element.** A card with a link in its title is one stop for a screen reader user, rather than one for every line inside it.
- **Hide what repeats.** If something is already said in text, hide the visual copy with `aria-hidden`.
- **Hide visually, not from assistive technology,** with `kicl-hidden`, when a label is only needed by people who can't see the layout.
pattern_screen_readers_intro: A screen reader turns the page into speech or braille. People move through it element by element, or jump by headings, links, landmarks and form fields. What they hear for each element is built from four things the browser works out from the markup.
pattern_screen_readers_leave_focus_alone:
## Leave focus alone, mostly

Let focus follow the page. Move it only when the context changes under the person:

- **On a route change,** move focus to the main content, so the new page is read from the top.
- **When a dialog opens,** focus moves into it. Native `dialog` does this.
- **When it closes,** focus goes back to the control that opened it. Native `dialog` and `popover` do this too.
- **Escape closes** a dialog, sheet or popover that can be closed, and leaves the person where they were.
pattern_screen_readers_name_everything:
## Name everything

Every control needs a name a person could say out loud, which also helps voice control users, as long as the name includes the visible text.
pattern_screen_readers_name_role_state_a:
## Name, role, state and description

- **Name:** what it's called. It comes from the text inside, a `label`, `alt` or `aria-label`.
- **Role:** what kind of thing it is, from the element: `button`, `a`, `input`, `h2`.
- **State:** what it's doing now: `checked`, `disabled`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-current`.
- **Description:** anything more, from `aria-describedby`, such as a field's hint or error.

A native element sets the role and state itself. `<button disabled>Save</button>` is read by VoiceOver as "Save, button, dimmed" with nothing extra. That's why the design system's components render the real element, and add ARIA where HTML can't express something.
pattern_screen_readers_part_4: Icons beside text are decorative, so they get `aria-hidden` and aren't read twice.

pattern_selection_intro: Selection lets people make a choice and see what's chosen. The right control depends on how many options there are and whether the choice takes effect straight away.
pattern_selection_keyboard:
## Keyboard

The native controls bring the keyboard with them. Arrow keys move between radios and segments, Space toggles a checkbox or switch, and typing a letter jumps through a select. A custom control has to rebuild all of that, which is the main reason to start from the real element.
pattern_selection_picking_the_control:
## Picking the control

- **One of a few:** `RadioGroup`. All the options stay visible, so people can compare them.
- **One of many:** `Select`, or `Combobox` when typing to filter is faster than scrolling.
- **Any number:** `CheckboxGroup`.
- **A view of the same content:** `Segmented`. It changes the view straight away.
- **A setting that applies at once:** `Switch`. If it waits for a form to be sent, use a `Checkbox`.
pattern_selection_preset_on_or_off: A `Switch` for a setting that applies the moment it changes, with a line that says what it means now.
pattern_selection_preset_one_of_a_few_pa: Pick a size. A `RadioGroup` keeps every option on screen, and the price under it follows your choice.
pattern_selection_preset_one_of_many_par: Pick a country. A `Select` keeps a long list out of the way, and the delivery estimate updates.
pattern_selection_preset_several: Pick any toppings, or none. A `CheckboxGroup` allows any number, and the summary keeps count.
pattern_selection_preset_switch_a_view: Switch between a list and a grid. A `Segmented` control changes how the same items are shown, straight away.
pattern_selection_references:
## References

- [WCAG 2.2, 1.4.1 Use of Color](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html)
- [WCAG 2.2, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
- [W3C WAI, Radio group pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/radio/)
- [W3C WAI, Switch pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/switch/)
pattern_selection_showing_whats_selected:
## Showing what's selected

The selected option has to stand out without color alone. Each of these controls pairs color with something else: a filled dot, a check, a moved thumb, a filled block behind the chosen segment. Those marks need at least 3:1 contrast against what's next to them.
pattern_states_availability:
## Availability

- **Read-only** for a value people should see and copy but not change.
- **Disabled** for a control that doesn't apply right now. Tab skips it, so a keyboard user may never reach it or learn why it's off. Say why, or leave the control out.
- Inside a form, keep the submit button enabled and explain what's missing instead.
pattern_states_content_states:
## Content states

- **Loading:** placeholders the shape of the content, so the layout doesn't jump. Mark the area `aria-busy` while it fills.
- **Empty:** say why it's empty and what to do next.
- **Error:** say what went wrong and how to recover. See [Feedback and status]({{docs}}patterns/interaction/feedback-and-status).
pattern_states_interaction_states:
## Interaction states

- **Hover** shows something can be used. It's a hint, never the only way to find something, since touch screens and keyboards don't hover.
- **Focus** shows where the keyboard is. It's a dashed outline on `:focus-visible`, so it shows for the keyboard and not for every click.
- **Pressed** confirms the click landed.
- **Selected** or **current** marks the chosen option or the page you're on, with `aria-current='page'` on links.
pattern_states_intro: A state tells people what a component is doing or what they can do with it. Each one should be clear without relying on color, and most of them come from the browser.
pattern_states_preset_empty: An empty list says why it's empty and offers the next step. Add an order to fill it, and Clear to empty it again.
pattern_states_preset_loading: The orders load when the card appears, and Reload loads them again. Placeholders the shape of the list hold its place, so nothing jumps when it arrives, and `aria-busy` tells assistive technology to wait.
pattern_states_preset_read_only_and_disa: Read-only can still be focused and copied: try the copy button. Disabled can't be reached at all, so the line under it says why. Turn on Pro plan to enable it.
pattern_understanding_disability_a_misma:
## A mismatch, not a condition

Since 2001 the World Health Organization has described disability as an interaction between a person's health and their environment, not only as something a person has. For a wheelchair user, the barrier is the stairs, not the wheelchair. Someone who can't see a screen is only shut out by an interface that has to be seen.

That moves the problem to where we can do something about it. We can't change someone's body, but we can change the page. Every time an interface assumes its user can see, hear, use a mouse, read quickly or hold still, it creates a mismatch for someone.
pattern_understanding_disability_intro: Accessibility starts with how you think about disability. It's often shortened to a11y, for the eleven letters between the first _a_ and the last _y_.
pattern_understanding_disability_permane:
## Permanent, temporary and situational

Disabilities differ in kind, in how severe they are and in how long they last. Kat Holmes and Microsoft's inclusive design team describe the last one as a spectrum: permanent, temporary and situational. For each kind, in that order:

- **Moving:** one arm, a broken wrist, or holding a child.
- **Seeing:** blind, dilated pupils, or bright sunlight.
- **Hearing:** deaf, an ear infection, or a loud train.
- **Thinking:** dementia, concussion, or constant interruptions.
- **Speaking:** non-verbal, laryngitis, or speaking a second language.

Designing for the permanent case often helps with the temporary and situational ones too. A page that works with one hand works for the parent holding a child, and captions written for deaf viewers help everyone on a loud train.
pattern_understanding_disability_referen:
## References

- [World Health Organization, International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/international-classification-of-functioning-disability-and-health)
- [Microsoft, Inclusive Design](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/)
- [Kat Holmes, Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262539487/mismatch/)
- [W3C WAI, Accessibility Principles](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-principles/)
pattern_understanding_disability_solving:
## Solving the edges improves the middle

Some everyday technologies grew out of accessibility work. Talking books were recorded for blind readers, many of them soldiers blinded in the First World War. The multi-touch gestures on today's touchscreens came from FingerWorks, whose co-founder had repetitive strain injury and needed a gentler way to type. When the hard cases work, the common case usually gets better too.

On the web, the same idea is why this system starts from native elements. A real `button` already works with a keyboard, a screen reader, voice control and a switch device. A `div` with a click handler works with a mouse, and every other way in has to be rebuilt by hand.
patterns_home_intro:
Patterns show how components work together to solve a common problem: telling someone what happened, asking for information, picking from options, or pausing a task to confirm it. Each one starts from what the browser already does and adds as little as it can.

The first group is about building for everyone from the start. Much of it comes from choosing the right element and writing clear content, which is easier at the start than as a fix later.
popover_intro: A small panel that opens next to its trigger. It uses the browser's own popover, so clicking outside or pressing Escape closes it.
popover_preset_a_link_with_a_hint: For a link with a note on what's behind it. Hovering or focusing it shows the hint, and clicking still follows the link.
popover_preset_basic: For a bit of extra information people open when they want it, like when something was last saved.
popover_preset_button_trigger: Opens from a real button, like an Options menu. `asChild` on `PopoverTrigger` makes your `Button` the trigger instead of wrapping it in another one.
popover_preset_hint: A short note that shows while the trigger is hovered or focused, like a tooltip.
popover_preset_inline: For a note on a word or phrase in a sentence. The trigger sits in the line and wraps with the words around it.
radio_group_intro: Pick one option from a short list where every option is visible.
radio_group_preset_basic: For a choice people have to make themselves. No option is picked until they click one.
radio_group_preset_in_a_form: For a choice a form needs made. The legend names the group, so it goes in a `FormItem` with its message rather than taking a label.
radio_group_preset_one_chosen: Starts with an option already picked, for when there's a sensible default.
radio_group_preset_one_option_disabled: For an option people should see but can't pick right now, like express delivery when it isn't offered.
radio_group_preset_with_an_error: For a choice nobody made yet. Every circle and the message turn red, and the message describes the whole group.
scroll_indicator_intro: A thin bar along the top of the window that fills as the page scrolls. Here it sits in a box that scrolls instead, with `position: sticky` so it stays at the box's top.
scroll_indicator_preset_basic: Scroll the text and the bar at the top fills up to show how far you are.
segmented_intro: Pick one of a few options shown side by side, like a view or a time range. The highlight slides to the chosen one.
segmented_preset_a_dropdown_when_narrow: At tablet width and below, it shows only the current choice and opens the rest in a popover. It starts collapsed here so you can see it.
segmented_preset_basic: For switching between a few views, like list, grid and map. It stays one row at every screen size.
segmented_preset_icons: For choices an icon says well, like light and dark. Give each option an `aria-label` so screen readers can tell them apart.
segmented_preset_in_a_form: For a choice in a form. Its legend names it, and the chosen value goes in the form's values like any field's.
segmented_preset_many_options: Six months fit in a row on a wide screen. At tablet width and below, the row scrolls sideways instead.
segmented_preset_nothing_chosen: Before anything is picked, no option is highlighted.
segmented_preset_scrolls_when_narrow: For a long list like the months of the year. They stay on one row that scrolls sideways.
segmented_preset_with_a_legend: Puts a visible label above the options. A `{'<legend>'}` as the first child names the group, so it doesn't need an `aria-label`.
select_intro: Pick one option from a list that's too long to show at once. It's a native `select`, styled where the browser supports `appearance: base-select`. `label` puts its name above it and `description` a hint below.
select_preset_basic: A plain dropdown. The first option is picked until someone changes it.
select_preset_groups: Splits a long list under headings, like cities by region.
select_preset_in_a_form: For a choice in a form. Saving with nothing chosen shows the error under it.
select_preset_inline: For a choice inside a sentence. Without its box, the select reads as the chosen value followed by an arrow, in the size and colour of the text around it.
select_preset_one_option_busy: For an option that is being prepared and can't be picked yet. Where the browser styles the select, a spinner shows beside it.
select_preset_one_option_disabled: For an option people should see but can't pick right now.
select_preset_parts_written_out: The same select with its parts written out: `SelectTrigger` holding `SelectValue`, then `SelectContent` around the options.
select_preset_with_a_label: For a choice with its name above it and a hint below.
select_preset_with_a_placeholder: Shows a prompt until something is picked, so the field doesn't start on a real answer. The prompt isn't one of the options.
select_preset_with_an_error: For a choice that has to be made and wasn't, with the reason under it.
separator_intro: A line between two things. It renders a `<span>` that screen readers skip. Where the line marks a change of topic, use `is='hr'`: it looks the same and is announced as a separator.
separator_preset_a_thematic_break: For a change of topic between paragraphs. As an `hr`, screen readers announce it.
separator_preset_basic: Splits stacked content, like two parts of a card, with a line across.
separator_preset_between_words: For a line between things side by side, like details in a row.
sheet_intro: A panel that slides in from an edge of the page, the end of the line by default. By default the page stays usable behind it. With `modal`, or on screens up to tablet width, where it fills the screen, it opens as a modal and the page behind can't be used.
sheet_preset_basic: A panel of filters that opens from the Open button. The button in its header closes it, and so does Escape.
sheet_preset_footer: For editing something and then saving it, with Cancel and Save at the bottom.
sheet_preset_long_content: For more than fits. The header and footer stay in place while the content scrolls between them.
sheet_preset_not_closable: There’s no close button and Escape does nothing, so your own code decides when it closes, like the Done button here.
skeleton_intro: A placeholder in the shape of content that's still loading, so the page doesn't jump when it arrives.
skeleton_preset_avatar: Stands in for a profile picture.
skeleton_preset_avatar_and_photo: For a block with more than one piece, like an avatar beside a photo. Use one skeleton per piece, laid out the way the content will be.
skeleton_preset_basic: Stands in for a photo or video while it loads.
skeleton_preset_lines_of_text: With no size of its own, a skeleton is one line of text tall, for lines still loading.
skeleton_preset_square: Stands in for a thumbnail or icon.
spinner_intro: Shows that something is loading. Screen readers hear "Loading" unless you pass a `label`.
spinner_part_2: `in` says whether the spinner shows, and defaults to on. When the load finishes, turn it off instead of unmounting the spinner, so it can animate out. Over its parent, the blurred layer comes in before the icon and leaves after it. Pick _Over its parent_ and toggle `in` to see both.
spinner_preset_basic: Sits in a line of text, next to a word like Loading.
spinner_preset_over_its_parent: Covers a card with a light blur and a spinner while its content loads.
status_intro: A short title and message about how something went: an error, a warning or information. A message without a title shows the level's icon in front of it. With neither, the level's default title shows, such as "Something went wrong" for an error.
status_part_2: `headingLevel` sets where the title sits in the page outline, from `h1` to `h6`. The title keeps the `h4` size at every level, so the toggle changes the code and the markup but not the look.
status_preset_basic: A one-line error, like a message that failed to send.
status_preset_only_a_level: With no title or message, the level's own title shows.
status_preset_with_a_title: A note after saving, with a short title over the message.
switch_intro: On or off for a setting that applies at once, such as the dark theme.
switch_preset_basic: The usual switch, with its name as text beside it. Clicking the text flips it too.
switch_preset_dark_theme: Turns this preview dark. The code shows the same switch wired to `useResponsive` for the whole site.
switch_preset_label_as_a_child: For a name that needs its own styling.
switch_preset_no_visible_label: For when the setting's name is already on screen nearby. `aria-label` gives the switch a name for screen readers.
table_intro: A native `<table>` for data that reads across rows and down columns. Write its `caption`, `thead`, `th` and `td` as you would in HTML. The table adds the rules between rows, the spacing and the header weight.
table_preset_basic: Column headers in a `thead`, one row per item, and a `caption` that names the table.
table_preset_row_headers: When the first cell names its row, make it a `th` with `scope='row'`. Screen readers then read it with every cell in the row. It keeps the body's weight, so the column headers still stand out.
text_intro: Body copy, and the inline elements inside it. `is` picks the element, so the markup says what the text is.
text_preset_a_code_block: For lines of code, kept as written.
text_preset_a_quote: For a quote that stands on its own. A line down its side sets it apart from the text around it.
text_preset_an_edit: Shows a change in place, with the old text struck through and the new text after it.
text_preset_basic: A single paragraph of body copy, which is what you get when you leave out `is`.
text_preset_code_with_a_look: Colours a status so it reads at a glance.
text_preset_inline: For words inside a sentence that need their own markup, like a command to type or a word to stress.
text_preset_paragraphs: Paragraphs that follow each other get a little space between them.
textarea_intro: A text field for more than one line, like a message or a note. `label` puts its name above it and `description` a hint below.
textarea_preset_basic: Before anyone has typed, the placeholder shows a hint.
textarea_preset_filled: With a reply already in it. The field grows taller as the text gets longer.
textarea_preset_in_a_form: For a message in a form, with a length rule on the `FormField`. Sending it empty or too long shows the error under it.
textarea_preset_taller: For notes or longer answers. It starts ten lines tall and still grows past that.
textarea_preset_with_a_label: For a message with its name above it and a hint below.
textarea_preset_with_a_limit: For a bio or anything else with a length cap. Typing stops at 160 characters and the count under the field keeps track.
textarea_preset_with_an_error: For a message that failed a check, with the reason under it.
token_breakpoints_intro: Each breakpoint is the top of its range: `narrow` is up to 352px, `mobile` up to 480px, and so on. `useResponsive` reads them in script.
token_breakpoints_part_5: A stylesheet reads them with `@container style(--kicl-viewport-up-to-desktop: true)`.
token_breakpoints_part_7: `kicl-hidden-up-to-{name}` visually hides an element at that width and narrower, and leaves it for screen readers. `{name}` is `narrow`, `mobile`, `tablet`, `desktop`, `wide` or `wider`.

### viewport

MDN: [`@container`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@container).

A media query can't read a custom property, so these flags say which range the window is in for a style query to read. `--kicl-viewport-{name}` is `true` inside that range, and `--kicl-viewport-up-to-{name}` is `true` at that width and narrower.
token_color_body_and_surface:
## Body and surface

Four roles cover most of the page. `--kicl-body-color` is text and `--kicl-body-background-color` is the page behind it. `--kicl-surface-color` is anything raised off the page, like a card, a popover or a field, and `--kicl-surface-border-color` is its edge. A surface is a short step away from the background, lighter on both themes, so it reads as raised.

`kicl--theme--light` and `kicl--theme--dark` set these roles. Components don't know which theme they're in. They read the roles, so the same card below takes both themes without a prop.
